reading.rtitle: The Five Minutes That Decide the Hour
paras: Most quarterly reviews are an hour long, and almost all of them are decided in the first five minutes. That is not a rule anybody wrote down. It is simply what happens: by minute six the room has already formed a view of whether the person speaking has the situation under control, and everything after that is read through it.

A good five minutes has the same shape everywhere. It opens with an overview and a promise of how many parts there are, so the room knows when it will end. It gives the headline number early, with the context that makes it mean something. It explains what moved and why, in one chain and not three. It names the decision, and the price of the decision, out loud.

And it finishes with the ask. This is the part that disappears most often, and almost always for the same reason: the person runs out of time or out of air, and the meeting closes without a decision. Presenters who work in a second language lose it more than anybody, not because their vocabulary fails, but because the structure does. They spend their energy on the middle and arrive at the end with nothing left.

The advice that fixes it is unfashionable and it works. Prepare two sentences word for word: the first one and the last one. Improvise everything between them. Speak more slowly than feels natural, and leave a silence between the parts, because a room reads silence as control. Then say the ask, and stop talking.
reading.source: A composite of guidance given to senior presenters, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain how long a quarterly review should be.
To show what a good five-minute update contains, and which part people lose first.
To argue that presentations should be improvised rather than prepared.

listenings.text: Good morning. Let me give you an overview first, and then the numbers. There are three things, and I will finish with what I need from you. The headline number is four point two per cent. For context, the baseline was three point one, and this is the largest book in the region and the fastest growing, so a number that looks bad in a table looks different once you know that. Second, why it moved. It moved because the April cohort reached its third payment this month. We ruled out the model in the first hour, so the policy was the next place to look. Third, the decision. We are tightening the rule again, and the trade-off is two quarters of growth. If you remember one thing from this, the takeaway is that the rate is one cohort, not the portfolio, and it is already handled. What I need from you is one signature from risk this week. That is the only blocker.

When somebody presents in a second language, the first thing they lose is not the vocabulary. It is the structure. The signals go: the sentence that tells the room what is coming, the one that says how many parts there are, the one that says this is the end. All the information is still there, and the room still cannot follow it, and the presenter walks out thinking their English is the problem. Two things fix most of it. The first is slower. The people who sound most senior in any language are the ones who leave a silence between the parts, and a second language gives you a perfect excuse to take that silence. The second is this: prepare two sentences word for word, the first one and the last one. Not the whole thing. Two. Everything in the middle can be improvised, because you know the content better than anybody in the room. It is the beginning and the end where nerves take the words away, so those are the ones you write down.
